## 17. Second-pass logic errors — the files the audit could not read

> **CLOSED.** This second pass was the largest single input to the 2026-08-18 fix wave; see **§B.2**, **§B.6**, **§B.7** and **§B.9**. Its own two headline faults - the un-converted lapse rate and the forgotten hardness run - were already closed on 2026-08-17.

**Scope:** `Climate.cpp`, `Weather.cpp`+`Weather.hpp`, `Biome.cpp`, `TerrainGenerator.cpp`, `Structures.cpp`, `Village.cpp` (549–1330), `ItemEntity.cpp`, `Recipe.cpp` (239–1030), `Tool.cpp` (70–773 and the `harvestTier` tail), `Settings.cpp`, `Sounds.cpp`, `Gamepad.cpp`, `Effects.hpp`, `Survival.hpp`, `Farming.hpp`, `Material.hpp`, `Buffer.cpp`, `UploadContext.cpp`, `GpuMemory.cpp`. Nothing was built or run; every line quoted below was read in the tree.

**Headline:** This code is *better* than the code §4 and §13 covered — the constant tables are unusually disciplined, world generation is provably deterministic, and `Settings.cpp` clamps every numeric setting it parses. The worst thing found is that **the weather system carries the reference's altitude lapse rate un-converted while the terrain generator carries the converted one**, so four biomes generate snow-capped and then get rained on, in the same column, forever. Behind it sit two more gaps of the shape this project keeps paying for: `blockHardness` names five of the six extra block runs and forgets the sixth (42 blocks, including the beacon and the monster spawner, silently priced at 1.0), and `Sounds.cpp`'s material table is the drifted half of a twin whose other half — `Material.hpp` — has all four of the rules it is missing.

### 17.1 Findings, ranked by player impact

#### F17.1 — Weather uses the reference's altitude lapse rate; terrain uses the converted one. They disagree about four biomes · `Weather.hpp:56-57` vs `Climate.cpp:268-270` · confidence: **certain**
- **What a player sees:** rain — not snow — falling on the snow-capped taiga and windswept hills that the world generated white, snow that never settles there during a storm, and lightning striking the frozen peaks.
- **Evidence:** two functions answer "does this column freeze", both from `Biome::warmth`, with different arithmetic.

```cpp
// Climate.cpp:265-284 — the converted one.
    // Every number here is the reference's own, in the reference's own units,
    // because `warmth` is too. Only the vertical scale is converted: its sea
    // level + 17 is our y 29, and one of our blocks covers 3.57 of its own.
    constexpr float kFreezePoint = 0.15f;
    constexpr float kLapseBase = 29.0f;
    constexpr float kWorldScale = 0.28f;
    constexpr float kLapsePerBlock = 0.00125f / kWorldScale;      // = 0.004464
    ...
    return warmth - (altitude + jitter * kJitterBlocks) * kLapsePerBlock < kFreezePoint;
```
```cpp
// Weather.hpp:54-57 — the un-converted one.
/// Temperature lost per block above y 81. Our world is short enough that this
/// only ever matters on a peak, which is exactly where it should.
constexpr float kWarmthPerBlock = 0.00125f;
constexpr float kWarmthBaseHeight = 81.0f;
```
```cpp
// Weather.cpp:49-52
    const float lapse =
        std::max(0.0f, static_cast<float>(surfaceY) - kWarmthBaseHeight) * kWarmthPerBlock;
    const float warmth = biomeInfo(biome).warmth - lapse;
    return warmth < kFreezingWarmth ? Precipitation::Snow : Precipitation::Rain;
```
And the table that owns `warmth` states, in its own doc comment, that there is only one reader:
```cpp
// Biome.hpp:185-187
    /// Only `freezesAt` reads it. Anything at or below 0.15 is white at sea
    /// level; above about 0.42 nothing in a world this short can ever chill it
    /// enough, which is why plains at 0.8 cannot whiten at any altitude.
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `kWarmthBaseHeight = 81.0f` is the *reference's* y (its sea level 63 + 18) dropped into a world whose sea level is 24 and whose tallest surface is `kMaxSurface = 90` (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:27`). The altitude term is therefore dead below y 81 and worth at most `9 × 0.00125 = 0.011` above it. The doc's own "above about 0.42" cut-off is `freezesAt`'s: `0.15 + (90 − 29) × 0.004464 = 0.42`. Weather's equivalent cut-off is `0.15 + 0.011 = 0.161`. **Every biome whose `warmth` falls in (0.161, 0.42] generates frozen at altitude and gets told it is raining** — Stony Shore 0.2, Windswept Hills 0.2, Gravelly Hills 0.2, Taiga 0.25 (`Biome.cpp`). Taiga crosses `freezesAt` at y ≈ 51; it would need y ≈ 161 to cross `precipitationFor`, which the world cannot reach. `precipitationFor` also drops `freezesAt`'s ±2.24-block jitter, so even where the two agree the runtime snow line is a clean contour against a ragged generated one. Consequences compound: `Main.cpp:6712` uses `precipitationFor` as the sole gate on snow settling, and `Weather.cpp:170` requires `Precipitation::Rain` before a bolt may land — so lightning strikes ice.
- **Fix shape:** delete `kWarmthPerBlock`/`kWarmthBaseHeight` and have `precipitationFor` call `freezesAt(seed, biomeInfo(biome).warmth, x, surfaceY, z)` — one owner, one lapse rate, jitter included. It needs the seed and the column, which the two call sites already have.

> **Fixed 2026-08-17, with one owner and a whole-derivation assert.** `weather::kWarmthPerBlock` is now the only altitude lapse rate in the tree, converted once for our 96-tall world, and `freezesAt` reads it — so the generator and the sky cannot disagree about which biomes freeze. The `static_assert` beside it checks the **whole** `freezingHeight()` expression the real reader evaluates, rather than one side of the derivation against itself, which is the trap `CLAUDE.md` #11 names. Two knock-ons were fixed with it: `precipitationFor` gained a five-argument form that asks `freezesAt` *with* the terrain jitter for anything that has a real column, and snow settling now uses that form instead of the jitter-free contour it used to disagree with the ground about.

#### F17.2 — `blockHardness` names five of the six extra block runs; the sixth falls to `default: return 1.0f` · `Tool.cpp:171-173` and `:506` · confidence: **certain**
- **What a player sees:** a beacon, a conduit, a monster spawner, a dragon egg, an end portal frame, a trapped chest and a blast furnace all come apart in about a second and a half, and tinted glass takes three times longer than plain glass.
- **Evidence:** the function knows exactly why this matters, for run 5:
```cpp
// Tool.cpp:171-173
    // The fifth run. **Named rather than left to the default**, because the
    // default is 1.0 and half of this run is either rock or wood.
    if (block >= kFirstExtraBlock5 && block <= kLastExtraBlock5) {
```
There is no counterpart for run 6 anywhere in `blockHardness`. `harvestTool` has one (`Tool.cpp:635`); `blockHardness` does not, so all 42 ids reach:
```cpp
// Tool.cpp:505-507
    default:
        return 1.0f;
    }
```
Mechanical proof — occurrences of each run-6 id in the whole of `Tool.cpp`:
```
Beacon 0   Conduit 0   MonsterSpawner 0   DragonEgg 0   EndPortalFrame 0
TrappedChest 0   BlastFurnaceExtra 0   TintedGlass 1 (harvestTool only)
```
Run 6 is `Candle .. BlastFurnaceExtraLast` (`Block.hpp:1172-1173`), 42 enumerators: 17 candles, TintedGlass, Beacon, Conduit, DragonEgg, EndPortalFrame, MonsterSpawner, 4 trapped chests, 7 blast-furnace states.
- **Why it is wrong:** Bedrock gives beacon/conduit/dragon egg 3.0, monster spawner 5.0, blast furnace 3.5, trapped chest 2.5, tinted glass 0.3, end portal frame unbreakable. Every one is priced at 1.0. This is a **different function** from the already-reported §13.5 (`harvestTier`, which decides *tier and drops*); this one decides *speed*, and the two gaps compound: a spawner is both 5× too fast and hand-tiered. The 17 candles are saved only by accident — `blockShape` calls them `Cross`, so the flat/cross early-out at `:130` catches them first.
- **Fix shape:** add a `kFirstExtraBlock6..kLastExtraBlock6` branch to `blockHardness` mirroring `:171`, and make the two defaults distinguishable in a debug build so the next missing run is loud.

> **Fixed 2026-08-17.** Run 6 has a branch and the 42 blocks are priced. Read this one beside §13.5, though: `blockHardness` is now total over the runs and **`harvestTier` still is not** — runs 1, 3, 4 and 7 have no branch, so a block can now be correctly slow to break and still drop for a bare hand. Two tables, the same shape of hole, one of them closed.

#### F17.3 — `Sounds.cpp`'s material table is the drifted half of a twin; four sound families are unreachable · `Sounds.cpp:198`, `:206`, `:209`, `:223` · confidence: **certain**
- **What a player sees and hears:** the entire surface of every snowy biome clacks like stone, all sixteen wools sound like chopping wood while the carpet cut from them correctly thumps, coral rustles like grass, and every ladder climb sounds like rock.
- **Evidence:** `Material.hpp` and `Sounds.cpp` write the same rules; `Sounds.cpp` has the narrower half of four of them.

| rule | `Material.hpp` | `Sounds.cpp` |
|---|---|---|
| snow | `id == Snow \|\| isSnowLayer(id)` (`:187`) | `block == BlockId::Snow` (`:198`) |
| cloth | `isWoolBlock(id) \|\| isCarpet(id)` (`:169`) | `isCarpet(block)` (`:209`) |
| wood | `… \|\| isLadder(id)` (`:166`) | no `isLadder` anywhere in the file |
| soil | `Grass\|Dirt\|CoarseDirt\|Podzol\|Mycelium` (`:190`) | `Grass \| Dirt` only (`:206`) |

```cpp
// Sounds.cpp:220-223 — and this is why none of it ever surfaced.
    // Wood is the only family broad enough to be worth a second test; every
    // remaining block is some kind of rock, which is also the safest thing for
    // an unknown to be.
    return isFlammable(block) ? SoundMaterial::Wood : SoundMaterial::Stone;
```
`SoundMaterial::Coral` is separately unreachable: `isCrossBlock` was widened to cover `isCoralPlant`/`isCoralFan` (`Block.hpp:1460`), so coral now hits the **Grass** early-out at `:206` before it can reach a coral test — bug shape #2 — and both `case SoundMaterial::Coral:` labels (`Sounds.cpp:244`, `:274`) are dead. `dig_coral`, `step_coral`, `step_ladder`, `dig_cloth` and `step_snow` are all staged, loaded into memory at startup, and can never play.
- **Why it is wrong:** shape #9 — the rule is correct and commented in exactly one of the two places that need it — with a `default:`-shaped fallback (shape #6) that makes "unmapped" and "genuinely stone" indistinguishable, so the drift produced no symptom a build or a soak could catch.
- **Fix shape:** have both tables call one shared set of predicates (`isSnowLike`, `isClothLike`, `isDirtLike`, `isWoodLike`), and add a startup probe that asserts every `SoundMaterial` enumerator is produced by at least one block id.

> **Fixed 2026-08-17.** `SoundMaterial` returns `Coral` and has a `Ladder`, so the fifteen staged recordings behind them can sound. The interesting part is *how* they were unreachable — not by a wrong branch but **by construction**, because the enumerator did not exist and no `switch` could name it, which is why every audio check ever run reported the files loaded and healthy. `LESSONS.md` has the general form: built, clean, and never called.

#### F17.4 — `kSteepDrop` is duplicated in `Structures.cpp` at the *pre-widening* value · `Structures.cpp:126` vs `TerrainGenerator.cpp:44-49` · confidence: **certain** (duplication) / **likely** (visible impact)
- **What a player sees:** trees growing out of bare cliff faces on mountainsides, exactly where the terrain painted stone because it called the slope steep.
- **Evidence:** the owner states the number *and* records that it was changed:
```cpp
// TerrainGenerator.cpp:44-49
/// How much a face must fall across two columns to count as steep.
/// The reference compares the height one step *north* against one step *south*
/// and asks for 4 over that span; ours is 96 blocks tall against its 384, so 2
/// is about the same fraction of the relief available.
constexpr int kSteepDrop = 2;
```
```cpp
// Structures.cpp:126-130
    constexpr int kSteepDrop = 4;
    return std::abs(surfaceHeightAt(seed, out.x - 1, out.z) - surface) < kSteepDrop &&
           std::abs(surfaceHeightAt(seed, out.x + 1, out.z) - surface) < kSteepDrop && ...
```
- **Why it is wrong:** two compounding errors. The literal is the abandoned 4, not the table's 2; and the *spans differ* — terrain measures across `z−1 → z+1` (two steps) and rejects at ≥ 2 (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:508`), while the tree measures **one** step from centre and permits up to 3, i.e. up to 6 across the same two-step span. Every slope terrain calls too steep for grass is happily planted on. Textbook shape #1: the range was narrowed and the old literal was not touched, and nothing changed type so the compiler could not help.
- **Fix shape:** export `kSteepDrop` from `TerrainGenerator.hpp` and reuse the same two-step comparison, not a four-way one-step test with its own constant.

> **Renamed 2026-08-17 — and the recommended fix was tried, reverted the same day, and is now rejected on the merits.** The two constants exist, they are `kSteepDropOverTwoColumns = 2` in `TerrainGenerator.cpp:59` and `kTreeSteepNeighbourStep = 4` in `Structures.cpp:140`, and **they answer different questions.** The generator asks for a *signed* fall across a two-column span — does the ground drop away in **this direction**, which is what makes a face bare rock and only makes sense with a direction. The tree gate asks for an *absolute* one-column step against **all four** neighbours — is this ground level enough to plant on, a question with no direction in it at all. Exporting one and reusing it, as recommended above, made far less bare stone on every peak in the world: a silent change to generated terrain, delivered inside a bug-fix session, in exchange for nothing a player would notice. What was actually wrong here was the **name**, not the value, and the names now say what each one measures. The finding stands as a correct observation with an incorrect prescription, and `LESSONS.md` records the shape: two constants with the same name are not necessarily one constant.
>
> The one part worth re-examining some day is this finding's second paragraph — that the two tests permit different amounts of fall across the same span. That is true, and it is a *design* question about how tolerant the tree gate should be, not a duplication to be merged away.

#### F17.5 — Ground cover vanishes on every column whose surface lands on y 31 or y 63 · `TerrainGenerator.cpp:665-668` · confidence: **certain**
- **What a player sees:** two razor-thin bald contour lines cut across every hillside — no grass, flowers, ferns, cactus, dead bush, berries or bamboo — at exactly y 31 and y 63.
- **Evidence:**
```cpp
// TerrainGenerator.cpp:665-673
            const int plantY = surface + 1 - baseY;
            if (plantY >= 1 && plantY < Chunk::kSize && surface > kSeaLevel + 1 &&
                chunk.at(x, plantY, z) == BlockId::Air &&
                chunk.at(x, plantY - 1, z) != BlockId::Air) {
                // Grows a stalk upward, stopping at the top of the chunk. A
                // stalk that runs off the top is simply shorter here; the cell
                // above belongs to another chunk and writing it from this one
                // would break generation purity.
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `Chunk::kSize == 32`. For `surface == 31`, the chunk at `baseY = 0` computes `plantY == 32` and fails `plantY < 32`; the chunk at `baseY = 32` computes `plantY == 0` and fails `plantY >= 1`. Neither plants it. The comment reasons carefully about the *upper* boundary and never about the lower one — shape #5, a derivation applied to one end of a pair. y 31 sits squarely between sea level 24 and `kMaxSurface` 90, so this is a visible seam across most of the world, not a corner case. (The `plantY - 1` support read is also `!= BlockId::Air` where `occludesFace`/`isOpaque` is the right question — shape #4.)
- **Fix shape:** when `plantY == 0`, do not consult the neighbouring chunk's cell — the support block is the known terrain top at world y `surface`; test the height map instead.

> **Fixed 2026-08-17, and it cost a format-version bump.** `plantY == 0` is now a real placement rather than the "nothing here" sentinel, so the bare bands at y 31/32 and y 63/64 are gone. Because the fix **changes generated terrain**, `kChunkFormatVersion` went 4 → 5: a saved chunk written under the old rule would sit beside a freshly generated neighbour that disagrees with it about ground cover, and the seam would be permanent. Note for anyone checking this by eye — merely standing near an ocean writes chunks to disk, because water flow calls `setBlock`, so a world that looks unfixed may simply be a world that was *loaded* rather than generated.

#### F17.9 — Village snow uses `occludesFace` with the sign inverted · `Village.cpp:1318` · confidence: **certain**
- **What a player sees:** in a snowy village, snow hovers a block above the slab-and-stair roofs, and any upper-half slab surface stays permanently bare.
- **Evidence:**
```cpp
// Village.cpp:1312-1322

                const BlockId here = w.chunk.at(lx, ly, lz);
                const BlockId above = w.chunk.at(lx, ly + 1, lz);

                if (!occludesFace(here, 1) || isSnowLayer(here)) { break; }
```
```cpp
// Block.hpp:5937-5953 — the offset is measured from the asking cell to the neighbour.
/// Whether a block one step away in `offsetY` fully hides the face it is pressed
/// against. ...
    case BlockShape::Slab:
        return isUpperHalf(neighbour) ? offsetY == -1 : offsetY == 1;
    case BlockShape::Stairs:
        return stairIsTop(neighbour) ? offsetY == -1 : offsetY == 1;
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `here` sits **below** the snow cell, so the correct query is `occludesFace(here, -1)`. Every other caller in the tree passes the offset *to* the neighbour (`ChunkMesher.cpp:348`, `:352`, `:794`; the `static_assert` at `Block.hpp:8182`). With `+1` the predicate answers the opposite question: it returns true for **bottom** slabs and stairs, whose top surface is half a block down and cannot hold flush snow, and false for **top** slabs, whose surface is flush and should. Full opaque cubes are unaffected (they ignore the offset), which is why this only shows on roofs — and every village roof is built with `slabAt(slabs, false)` / `stairsAt(..., false)`, i.e. bottom halves.
- **Fix shape:** `occludesFace(here, -1)`.

#### F17.11 — `veinHeight` picks *one of two* uniform rolls where its own comment specifies *the average of two* · `TerrainGenerator.cpp:353-364` · confidence: **certain**
- **What a player sees:** "dig to y 6 for diamond" buys much less than it should — diamond is uniformly scattered over y 6–17 half the time and crammed into y 3–6 the other half, instead of peaking at 6.
- **Evidence:**
```cpp
/// The reference's `trapezoid` height provider with a zero plateau, which is
/// just a triangle: the average of two uniform rolls. That is what makes a
/// depth feel like a depth rather than like a floor you cross.
int veinHeight(const OreVein& vein, noise::Stream& roll) {
    const int lowSpan = vein.peakY - vein.minY;
    const int highSpan = vein.maxY - vein.peakY;
    const int low = vein.minY + roll.range(std::max(1, lowSpan + 1));
    const int high = vein.peakY + roll.range(std::max(1, highSpan + 1));
    return roll.range(2) == 0 ? low : high;
}
```
- **Why it is wrong:** a 50/50 mixture of two uniforms is piecewise-uniform with a step discontinuity at `peakY` — the opposite of the triangle the comment promises, and it puts half of every ore's veins into whichever of the two bands is narrower. The triangular provider is `min + (range(span) + range(span)) / 2`.
- **Fix shape:** `return vein.minY + (roll.range(span) + roll.range(span)) / 2;` over the whole band, keeping the draw count the same so vein streams stay aligned across chunks.

#### F17.12 — Cloud cover cannot lead the rain, and `kCoverageLeadSeconds` is declared and never used · `Weather.cpp:122-125`, `Weather.hpp:66` · confidence: **certain**

- **Evidence:**
```cpp
// Weather.hpp:62-66
/// **Coverage leads the rain.** Clouds gather, then it rains; a deck that
/// thickens at the same moment the first drop falls reads as a slider being
/// dragged rather than as weather having a cause.
constexpr float kCoverageRampPerSecond = 0.03f;
constexpr float kCoverageLeadSeconds = 30.0f;
```

```cpp

    m_cloudLevel = approach(m_cloudLevel, rainTarget, kCoverageRampPerSecond, deltaSeconds);

```
`Select-String -Pattern 'kCoverageLeadSeconds'` across the whole tree → one hit, its own declaration.

The lead the header promises would need the cloud target to be driven off the rain countdown 30 s early, which is what the unused constant is for. | i | `Buffer`'s constructor destroys the buffer if the *allocation* fails, but if `vkBindBufferMemory` then fails, `vkCheck` throws after a successful sub-allocation and the destructor never runs — leaking both the `VkBuffer` and the `MemoryRange` | `Buffer.cpp:70-82` | certain |

### 17.2 Answers to the specific questions asked

- **`GpuMemory` invalid-range handling (audit §12.10): yes, the caller checks it, and it is handled correctly.** `Buffer.cpp` is the only caller of `allocateBufferMemory`, and it tests `range.valid()` immediately, cleans up the already-created `VkBuffer`, and throws — so a failed allocation is a clean exception, not silent corruption:
  ```cpp
  // Buffer.cpp:66-74
      const MemoryRange range =
          allocateBufferMemory(context.device(), context.physicalDevice(), requirements, memoryProperties);
      if (!range.valid()) {
          // The buffer already exists; without this it would leak on a failed allocation.
          vkDestroyBuffer(context.device(), m_buffer, nullptr);
          m_buffer = VK_NULL_HANDLE;
          throw std::runtime_error("vkAllocateMemory failed");
      }
  ```
  §12.10 can be closed as **not a bug**. Two riders worth recording: (1) the *next* line, `vkCheck(vkBindBufferMemory(...))`, throws from inside the constructor after a successful sub-allocation, so `~Buffer` never runs and both the buffer and the range leak — the guard exists in one of the two places that need it (finding **i** above); (2) `UploadContext` never handles the throw, so an out-of-memory during a chunk upload propagates out of `stage()` and kills the frame — acceptable, but it means the failure is fatal rather than degrading. `GpuMemory`'s pool is properly thread-safe (`g_poolMutex` held across both `allocateBufferMemory` and `freeBufferMemory`; `g_liveAllocations` is `std::atomic`), so nothing here is a race.
- **Determinism of world generation: clean.** Grepped `TerrainGenerator.cpp`, `Structures.cpp`, `Biome.cpp`, `Climate.cpp` and `Village.cpp` for `rand(`, `srand`, `random_device`, `mt19937`, `chrono`, `clock`, `time(`, `thread_local` and mutable file-scope state — **zero hits in all five**. Every draw comes from `noise::Stream` seeded by `hash2D(seed ^ salt, cellX, cellZ)` or from position-hashed `hashUnit2D`. The only `static` in the set is `Biome.cpp:365`, a `static const float` computed by a lambda purely from the `constexpr kBiomes` table, which is order-independent. Structures that straddle a chunk boundary agree: every `roll` draw is guarded only by conditions that are functions of the feature (`mega`, `dx`, `dz`, `radius`), never of the asking chunk, and `place()`/`Chunk::set` drop out-of-range writes *after* the draw; `placeVein` explicitly rolls its discard before the `Chunk::contains` test. `Village::solve()` never sees a chunk. **`Structures.cpp:431` is worth tidying but is not a determinism bug** — `for (int y = base + 1; y <= base + tree.height - roll.range(2); ++y)` re-draws the bound every iteration, burning `height` extra stream draws, but the count depends only on `tree.height`, so all chunks agree. (For contrast, `Main.cpp:6705` does use `std::rand()` — for snow settling, which is runtime gameplay, not generation.)
- **`settings.cfg` robustness: good — better than anything else audited.** A missing file is written with defaults. A malformed line without `=` is skipped. `parseUnsigned`, `parseInt` and `parseFloat` all reject rather than coerce (`parseFloat` requires `consumed == text.size()` *and* `std::isfinite`, so `1e999`, `nan`, `0x10` and `5abc` are all refused), a rejected value keeps the default and logs a warning, and **every** numeric setting is clamped after parsing (`Settings.cpp:227-254`): floats to explicit ranges, `renderDistance`/`detailDistance` to ≥ 1, `dayLengthSeconds` to ≥ 10, and the enum-like unsigneds to `kCount - 1`. `render_scale` is clamped to `[0.5, 1.0]` and clamped *again* in `Renderer::setRenderScale`. Two gaps only: `spawn_x`/`spawn_z` have neither a limit nor a clamp (finding **h**), and `creature_showcase` is the one setting parsed with `std::atoi` (`Settings.cpp:210`), bypassing the discipline the file's own comment exists to enforce — it is harmless today because `Main.cpp:2477` clamps it at the use site, but it is a rule that did not travel. **No hostile value found that crashes or produces an absurd world.**
- **Duplicate rows in `Recipe.cpp` / `Tool.cpp`: none in `Recipe.cpp`; none within any `switch` in `Tool.cpp`, but ten ids in `Tool.cpp` have two owners and one pair disagrees.** For recipes, normalising each literal to `kind|dimensions|ingredient cells` and grouping gave **103 keys, zero collisions**; a second pass confirmed no shaped recipe has an item count ≠ `w*h` and no shapeless one has a count ≠ its `used`. The matcher does return the first match in table order, but `matchesShapeless` ends `return filled == matched;` (no leftovers permitted) and `matchesShaped` requires an exact bounding-box match plus explicit empties, so a smaller recipe cannot shadow a larger one — first-match is safe here. For `Tool.cpp`, extracting `case BlockId::(\w+)` per switch region and grouping gave **no duplicate label in any of the ten regions** (the ~110 apparent duplicates in a naive whole-file group are each block appearing once in `blockHardness`, once in `harvestTool` and once in `harvestTier`, which is expected). The real duplication is F17.7: `Target`, `SculkVein`, `MossCarpet`, `NoteBlock`, `Leaves`, `Log`, `CrimsonStem`, `WarpedStem`, `MangroveLog` and `BambooBlock` each have a switch row *and* an earlier family predicate that already answered — one of each pair is dead code, and `Target` is outright contradictory at 0.5 vs 0.4.

### 17.3 Checked and found correct — do not re-spend the time

- **`Survival.hpp`'s drowning unit conversion is right**: `kDrownDamagePerSecond` is a rate but the caller converts it — `Player.cpp:258`, `static_cast<int>(kDrownDamagePerSecond * kHazardInterval + 0.5f)` → 1 point per 0.5 s = 2/s. It is deliberately outside the `kHazardInterval` `static_assert` for that reason.
- **`Survival.hpp`'s food table otherwise matches Bedrock** on all ~35 entries I checked; `foodTablesAgree()` is a genuine cross-table proof, not a self-comparison. `kInvulnerableSeconds = 0.5` = 10 ticks ✓; `kSafeFallDistance`, `kFireBurnSeconds`, `kLavaBurnSeconds`, `kRegenFoodFloor`, `kSprintFoodFloor`, `kStarveFloor` (Normal) and the exhaustion table are all correct.
- **`Farming.hpp` is the cleanest file in the set.** `kRandomTicksPerChunkPerTick = 8` is *correctly* derived: our 32³ chunk is eight of the reference's 16³ sections at Bedrock's 1 tick each → 8/32768 = 1/4096 per block per tick = the 204.8 s the comment quotes. `growthChance`'s `floor(25/points)+1` matches the reference and its three `static_assert`s are real checks against published probabilities.
- **`Effects.hpp` is clean.** Bedrock's ids, Bedrock's compound haste `(1+0.2n)·1.2ⁿ` (not Java's flat form), Bedrock's strength/weakness formulas, `50>>n` / `25>>n` / `40>>n` correctly expressed as 2.5 / 1.25 / 2.0 seconds. No unit error found; the `instantAmount` `static_assert` is a real check. Only nit: `effectInfo`'s `default:` returns `{"", false, 0xFFFFFF}`, which would render a nameless white effect rather than failing — low risk, the enum is closed.
- **`Weather.hpp`'s other units are right.** `kLevelRampPerSecond = 0.2` = the reference's 0.01/tick × 20 ✓. `kStrikeChancePerSecond = 201·20/100000` is documented as a re-derived *rate* rather than a ported per-chunk probability, and `roll() > rate * deltaSeconds` is frame-rate independent ✓. All four rain/thunder tick ranges match the reference and are converted by `× kTickSeconds` ✓.
- **`Gamepad.cpp` is clean** — the deadzone is normalised on both sides (`engine::GamepadAxes` is `float`, `Settings.hpp` default 0.2, clamped to [0, 0.6]), so there is no raw-int16-vs-normalised mix and no `-(-32768)` overflow; `applyDeadzone`/`applyCurve` both guard the zero-magnitude divide, so no NaN camera; look speed is `rad/s × deltaSeconds` and the caller *adds* rather than re-scaling; Y-inversion is applied once to both sticks; `platformButton` is proved total by a `static_assert`; `playRumble` bounds-checks its index.
- **`Sounds.cpp`'s array sizing is exact** — `kStems` = 60 against `SoundEvent`'s 60 + `Count`; `kVoiceStems` = 35 against `CreatureVoice`'s 35; `CreatureVoice::None` is guarded before it can index `m_voices`; every `pick`/`digSoundFor`/`stepSoundFor` path tests `!= SoundEvent::Count` at the call site. No out-of-bounds and no duplicate stem string in any of the three tables.
- **Negative coordinates are handled correctly throughout worldgen.** `Structures.cpp:529-532` and `Village.cpp` use `floorDivInt`; `TerrainGenerator.cpp:725-726` uses `worldX >> kFlowerRegionShift`, which *is* correct floor maths for a power of two. No raw `/ 16` or `% 16` on a signed coordinate exists in any of the five worldgen files. (`Village.cpp:1138`/`:1214`'s `/ 2` is the one exception — finding **e**.)
- **Village builder writes cannot go out of bounds** — everything funnels through `Writer::put` → `Chunk::contains`, and `Chunk::at/set/setWaterlogged` are bounds-checked, so roof overhangs, the foundation skirt and out-of-layer y values are clipped rather than written. `kMaxBuildings`/`kMaxRoads`/`kMaxDecor`/`kMaxResidents` are all tested before the post-increment; `plansNear`'s 4-plan cap cannot truncate (144-block window against a 448-block grid).
- **`Tool.cpp`'s inner `default: return 1.0f` at `:230` shadows nothing.** I checked whether any block named in the outer switch falls inside run 5 (`OakWood` 754 … `RespawnAnchor` 898) — `AncientDebris` is at 174, `Cobweb` 398, `Bedrock` 147, `Jukebox` 382, and so on; every outer case sits below 754. No hidden second `blockHardness` bug of the §13.5 shape.
- **`Tool.cpp` spot values are right**: obsidian 50, stone 1.5, planks 2.0, glass 0.3, bedrock 3600; `breakSeconds` is `hardness × penalty / speed` in *seconds*, matching the header, with no 20 Hz value mixed in. The deepslate-ore derivation (`blockHardness(stoneOreFor(block)) * 1.5f`) correctly avoids a second copy of the ore list. `isSmoker`/`isFurnace` are already split correctly in both `harvestTool` and `harvestTier`.
- **`Recipe.cpp`'s offset arithmetic is exact** — the nine waxed-copper ids, the ten bark logs and ten stripped forms all map 1:1 onto their `Block.hpp` runs with no off-by-one; the five tool patterns decode to the correct Bedrock shapes; the twelve flower→dye pairs and nine dye mixes are correct with no duplicate key.
- **`Biome.cpp` lookups are in bounds** — `biomeInfo` clamps with `std::min(index, kBiomes.size() - 1)`, `kBiomes` is `std::array<Biome, BiomeId::Count>` and the row count and order match the enum. `ClimateRange`'s NSDMIs default to `{-1, 1}` (any), not `{0, 0}`, so the 26 rows that omit `.weirdness` are unconstrained as intended.
- **`Climate.cpp`'s spline evaluator is correct** — Hermite basis with derivatives scaled by the span (not used raw), linear extrapolation outside the end points rather than a clamp, and the `while (i + 1 < N && ...)` search cannot run off the array. `ridgesFromWeirdness`, the shared warp, the per-field salts and the measured per-field gains are all internally consistent and documented against measurement. No divide-by-zero: every span is non-zero by construction and `smoothstep`'s divisor is a compile-time constant difference.
- **`TerrainGenerator.cpp`'s `heights` ring is exactly sized** (`kSpan = Chunk::kSize + 2 = 34`, consumers stay in `[-1, 32]`), the `switch (tree.variant)` has no `default:` so a new variant is a compile error, and `y` units are consistent — `freezesAt` and `isCave` receive world Y at every call site, and `plantY`/`bedY`/`caneY`/`padY` are consistently chunk-local and range-checked.
- **`ItemEntity.cpp`'s despawn compaction is safe** (swap-with-back while iterating downward), and its units are right: `kDespawnSeconds = 300` against an age accumulated in `deltaSeconds` is exactly Bedrock's 6000 ticks, and the water branch passes the per-tick `fluid::kWaterDrag` to `fluid::approach`, which converts it via `dragOver(drag, dt)` — no per-tick constant is multiplied by `dt`.
- **`UploadContext.cpp` is correct.** The arena offset can never exceed capacity in a way that overruns the mapped pointer (the overflow test runs before the copy and `bytes > m_arenaCapacity` is diverted to a dedicated buffer first); `m_oversized` is cleared only inside `recycleArena`, which waits on the fence first, so an oversized staging buffer is never destroyed while the GPU is reading it; `m_arena` and `m_oversized` are declared such that they are destroyed after the destructor's fence wait.
- **`Material.hpp` is clean** — every layer index is bounds-checked, `conflicts` is counted per distinct layer as documented, and the emissive min-claim rule matches its comment. Its only defect is a stale "sixteen rows" comment over a 17-row table.

### 17.4 Still unread

- `Village.cpp` 1–548 (the planner) was read only for context; `solve()`'s plot-packing loop and `plansNear`'s grid were checked for termination and bounds but not line by line.
- `Recipe.cpp` 1031–1297 (the matcher tail, furnace/smelting tables) — the matcher functions were read where the duplicate question required them; the smelting and stonecutter tables were not swept for Bedrock fidelity.
- `Biome.cpp`'s surface-rule bodies below the climate table, and `Climate.cpp`'s spline *values* — I verified the evaluator and the internal consistency of the tables, not that each of the 34 control points matches the reference's router.
- `Sounds.cpp`'s music scheduler and 3D attenuation beyond the constants; `AudioEngine.cpp` entirely (out of the assigned set).
- The hot–wet biome gap flagged by the terrain pass (`temperature > 0.55 && humidity > 0.30` on non-coastal land appears to be claimed by no row, so `biomeFor` exits via the nearest-box fallback) is **unresolved**: it needs `climateAt` sampled over a few thousand columns to say whether the region is real terrain or measure-zero. `worldgen_probe=1` already exists and would answer it in one run — but running it was out of scope here.

## 18. Animation and rig errors — the code the audit could not read

> **PARTLY CLOSED, and the only Part Two section that was NOT systematically re-verified.** Its headline *is* fixed: the per-creature animation phase is now seeded, so a reloaded world no longer sways in lockstep (`Creature.cpp:29-38` scatters `age` across `kAgePhaseSpan` and seeds the squid's `jetPhase` beside it). **The rig findings from F18.1 onward were not re-checked against the current tree and should be treated as open** until someone reads `Creature.cpp`'s rig code again.

**Scope:** `game/src/world/Creature.cpp` 5233–7888 (all of `Creatures::buildMesh` — frame setup, `boxAxes`/`uprightBox`/`legBox`/`barBox`/`lyingBox`/`finBox`/`heldItem`, the sway and attack curves, and every one of the 57 species rigs); the animation-state plumbing at 3811–3836 (`think`'s head ease), 3838–3900 and 4260–4330 (`step`'s gait/age/flap/stepSmooth), 4329–4400 (`update`); the pose-derivation constants and functions at 2073–2135 (`bipedHandPoint`, `villagerHandPoint`, `modelPointToWorld`), 2185–2270 (archer/witch constants, `archersShareOneRig`) and 2338–2390 (`loose`); the `kSpecies` gait/held/swing columns 635–1220; `Creature.hpp` 1014–1200 (animation fields); `Player.cpp` 15–30 and 892–950 (step easing); `ANIMATION.md` §1–§4 and `TEXTURING.md` §14.

**Headline:** The rig code is in much better shape than its size suggests — the pivot rule is derived from the box rather than authored, the head turns about a real neck with correct `remainder` wrapping and clamps, the diagonal trot is right on all thirteen quadrupeds, the spider matches `geometry.spider.v1.8` term for term, and animation phase is genuinely frame-time driven with per-tick constants correctly converted by `pow(k, dt/0.05)`. The worst thing found is the Princepin family: all three carry a weapon in the species table, the rig never calls `heldItem`, and the attack swing is bolted to the **left** arm while every other rig in the file — and `bipedHandPoint`'s own comment — puts the main hand on the right. Behind that sit two witch bugs (her wind-up moves the arms the wrong way, and the potion leaves ~0.38 blocks from where the bottle is drawn), and one whole-world bug: `creature.age` is documented as existing "so a crowd does not sway in unison" and is never seeded, so a freshly loaded world has every biped in exact phase.

---

### 18.1 Findings, ranked by what a player would see

#### F18.1 — The Princepin family swings its left arm and never draws its weapon · `Creature.cpp:7274–7283` (rig), `968–973 / 1146–1157` (table) · confidence: **certain**

- **What a player sees:** a Princepin, a Brute and a Zombified Princepin all attack **bare-handed with the wrong arm** — the left arm chops while the right arm keeps walking, and the stone sword / stone axe the species table says they carry is never drawn at all.
- **Evidence:**

```cpp
constexpr float kPigShoulder = 0.375f;
legBox(place(0.0f, 1.125f, kPigShoulder), 4.0f, 12.0f, 4.0f,
       32.0f, 48.0f, skin, 0.005f, -swing + swayPitch - humanoidRaise,
       swayRoll);
legBox(place(0.0f, 1.125f, -kPigShoulder), 4.0f, 12.0f, 4.0f,
       40.0f, 16.0f, skin, 0.005f, swing - swayPitch, -swayRoll);
continue;                       // <- no heldItem() anywhere in this branch
```

  `+side` is provably the creature's **left**: the `+kPigShoulder` arm reads net `(32,48)` — the player skin's *left arm* rect — and the `+kPigHip` leg reads `(16,48)`, the *left leg*. The `-side` pair read `(40,16)` and `(0,16)`, the right arm and right leg. Compare the general biped, which puts the same term on the opposite arm and says why:

```cpp
// **The swinging arm is the mob's right**, because that is the
// main hand and it is the hand an item is drawn in. It was the
// left until held items arrived...
mainPitch = blend(swing - swayPitch - humanoidRaise, aimPitch - swayPitch);
mainHand  = legBox(place(0.0f, kBipedArmRestUp, -shoulder), ...);
const ModelPoint grip = bipedHandPoint(limb, mainPitch, mainRoll, true);
heldItem(held, mainHand, false);
```

  And the table rows are unambiguous — all three have both flags set:

```cpp
{.name = "Princepin",        ... .swingsArms = true, .heldMainHand = ItemId::StoneSword},
{.name = "Princepin Brute",  ... .swingsArms = true, .heldMainHand = ItemId::StoneAxe},
{.name = "Zombie Princepin", ... .swingsArms = true, .heldMainHand = ItemId::StoneSword},
```

  The walk swing and the idle sway in this rig *are* correct and mirrored — only `humanoidRaise` sits on the wrong member of the pair. This is the project's #1 bug shape (a derivation applied to one of a pair and not the other) landing on left/right limb.
- **What the reference does:** Bedrock's `animation.humanoid.attack.rotations` drives `rightarm` only — `"rightarm": {"rotation": ["math.sin(1.0 - math.pow(1.0 - variable.attack_time, 3.0) * 180.0) * ...", ...]}` — and the held item bone is `rightitem`. Piglins, brutes and zombified piglins are all `geometry.piglin` with `minecraft:behavior.melee_attack` and a golden sword/axe in the main hand. <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZtechNetwork/MCBVanillaResourcePack/master/animations/humanoid.animation.json>
- **Fix shape:** move `- humanoidRaise` from the `+kPigShoulder` call to the `-kPigShoulder` call, capture that second call's `LimbEnd`, and add the `bipedHandPoint` + `heldItem` pair the biped helper already uses. **Do not implement.**

---

#### F18.2 — The witch's wind-up lowers her arms instead of raising them · `Creature.cpp:7088–7101` · confidence: **likely** (arithmetic is certain; the pose can only be confirmed by eye)

- **What a player sees:** in the 0.6 s before a witch throws, her folded arms **drop from chest height to hanging by her sides and slightly behind her**, and the bottle goes with them — the opposite of the overhand lob the constant's own comment describes.
- **Evidence:**

```cpp
constexpr float kFold = kVillagerFold;          // -0.75f
const float turn = -armRaise;                   // armRaise = creature.aim * 0.85f
const float cosTurn = std::cos(turn);
const float sinTurn = std::sin(turn);
const auto folded = [&](float alongForward, float up, float alongSide) {
    const float dy = up - kVillagerArmPivotUp;  // 1.384f
    return place(alongForward * cosTurn - dy * sinTurn,
                 kVillagerArmPivotUp + alongForward * sinTurn + dy * cosTurn,
                 alongSide);
};
uprightBox(folded(0.1477f, 1.221f, 0.375f), 4.0f, 8.0f, 4.0f,
           44.0f, 22.0f, skin, 0.005f, kFold + armRaise);
```

  The rotation is internally consistent — rotating the centre by `turn` and the pitch by `-turn` keeps the assembly rigid, which is what the comment promises. It is the **sign** that is wrong. Working the sleeve's lower face through:

  | | `armRaise = 0` | `armRaise = 0.85` (full) |
  |---|---|---|
  | box pitch | `-0.75` rad (43° forward of vertical) | `+0.10` rad (**vertical**) |
  | hands, alongForward | `0.318` | `-0.050` |
  | hands, up | `1.038` | `0.917` |

  "Straight out" for this rig is pitch `-1.5708` (that is what `kArcherArmPitch` is). The raise moves the pitch **toward zero**, i.e. toward hanging, and carries the hands backwards past the pivot and downwards. The stated intent is the reverse:

```cpp
/// How far the folded arms swing up over a throw, in radians. Taken with the
/// fold's own -0.75 it ends just past straight out, which is an overhand lob
/// rather than a punch...
constexpr float kWitchArmRaise = 0.85f;
```
- **What the reference does:** nothing to port — Bedrock ships no witch throw animation (`witch.entity.json` uses `animation.humanoid.*` plus the villager base pose only), which the constant's own doc block already says. The yardstick here is therefore the code's own stated intent, not the reference.
- **Fix shape:** flip both signs together — `turn = +armRaise` and box pitch `kFold - armRaise` — so the assembly and its pitch stay each other's inverse. **Do not implement.**

---

#### F18.3 — The witch's potion leaves ~0.38 blocks from where the bottle is drawn · `Creature.cpp:2338–2350` vs `7118–7126` · confidence: **certain**

- **What a player sees:** the splash potion pops out of the middle of the witch's chest, roughly half a block in front of and above the bottle visibly in her hands, at the exact instant she is most wound up.
- **Evidence:** `loose()` derives the origin from the **unrotated rest** hand point…

```cpp
// Both points come from the same two functions the mesh hangs the item on,
// so the arrow can only ever leave the bow and the bottle can only ever
// leave the fingers.
const glm::vec3 from =
    thrower ? modelPointToWorld(self, ctx.species, villagerHandPoint())
            : modelPointToWorld(self, ctx.species, bipedHandPoint(...));
```

  ```cpp
  ModelPoint villagerHandPoint() {                       // no armRaise parameter
      const float reach = kVillagerArmLength * kTexel;
      return {-std::sin(kVillagerFold) * reach,
              kVillagerArmPivotUp - std::cos(kVillagerFold) * reach, 0.0f};
  }
  ```

  …while the mesh draws the bottle at that same point **carried round by the swing**:

```cpp
const ModelPoint grip = villagerHandPoint();
const LimbEnd hands{folded(grip.alongForward, grip.up, 0.0f), gripUp, ...};
heldItem(ItemId::None, hands, false);
```

  Release happens at `creature.aim ≈ 1`, so `armRaise ≈ 0.85` and `folded()` has moved the drawn bottle from model `(0.341, 1.018)` to `(-0.050, 0.886)` — a separation of `0.413` model units, `×0.92` villager `modelScale` = **≈0.38 blocks (6 texels)**. The comment claiming the two agree is false for every non-zero `armRaise`, and it is the first entry in `CLAUDE.md`'s bug box: a value derived somewhere other than the one place that owns it.
- **What the reference does:** Bedrock spawns `minecraft:splash_potion` from the mob's held-item bone. There is no published number to port; the requirement is only that the two agree, which is what the code says it is doing.
- **Fix shape:** give `villagerHandPoint(float armRaise = 0.0f)` the same rotation `folded()` applies, and pass `self.aim * kWitchArmRaise` from `loose()`. Note this becomes *larger*, not smaller, once F18.2 is fixed. **Do not implement.**

---

#### F18.4 — `creature.age` is never seeded, so a herd sways in lockstep and a reloaded world snaps into unison · `Creature.hpp:1046–1048`, `Creature.cpp:4277` · confidence: **certain**

- **What a player sees:** load a save and **every zombie, villager, skeleton, Princepin, witch and axolotl in the world is in exact animation phase** — arms swaying identically, axolotl tails beating as one — and it stays that way. Freshly spawned groups (`groupSize` 2–4, spawned in one call) have the same problem from the moment they appear.
- **Evidence:** the field's own doc states the requirement:

```cpp
/// How long this individual has been alive, for idle motion that runs
/// whether or not it is going anywhere. Per creature rather than a world
/// clock so a crowd does not sway in unison.
float age = 0.0f;
```

  It is only ever incremented — `creature.age += deltaSeconds;` (4277) — and no `place`, `placeVillager`, `restore`, `populateChunks` or `manage` path ever offsets it. Everything idle rides on it:

```cpp
const float swayRoll  = std::cos(creature.age * 1.8f) * 0.05f + 0.05f;   // 5820
const float swayPitch = std::sin(creature.age * 1.34f) * 0.05f;          // 5821
const float sway = creature.inWater ? std::sin(creature.age * 5.0f) * 0.45f
                                    : std::sin(creature.age * 1.4f) * 0.08f;  // 7636
```

  `phaseDelay` is a **schedule** stagger, not an animation phase — its only reader is the day/night schedule at 3740. The correct rule already exists twenty lines from the increment, for one field only:

```cpp
// Seeded on the first tick rather than at construction, so a
// group of them is out of phase with itself.
if (creature.age <= 0.0f) {
    creature.jetPhase = random01() * kTwoPi;
}
```

  This is `CLAUDE.md` bug shape 14 in its purest form — a rule that exists, is correct, is commented, and travelled to one of the two places that need it. Worse, the squid's guard *depends* on `age` starting at zero, which is the very thing that breaks the sway.
- **What the reference does:** Bedrock's idle sway reads `query.life_time`, which is per-entity and starts when that entity spawns — `"rightarm": {"rotation": [0,0,"(math.cos(query.life_time * 103.2) * 2.865) + 2.865"]}` in `animation.humanoid.bob`. Because Minecraft entities are created at scattered ticks and `life_time` survives a save, a vanilla crowd is never in phase. <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZtechNetwork/MCBVanillaResourcePack/master/animations/humanoid.animation.json>
- **Fix shape:** seed `age` with `random01() * kTwoPi / 1.34f` (a full period of the slower term) at every spawn site, and persist it — or, cheaper, add one `phase` field seeded once and read `age + phase` in the four expressions above. **Do not implement.**

#### F18.5 — Biped arms swing at the legs' full amplitude; the reference gives them 1/1.4 of it · `Creature.cpp:6828–6832, 6861, 6895, 6902` (and `7096–7101`, `7279–7283`) · confidence: **certain** on the arithmetic

- **What a player sees:** every zombie, husk, drowned, skeleton, blackbone, villager, trader, witch and Princepin walks with its **arms swinging as far as its legs** — a stiff, marching gait rather than the reference's looser arm-behind-leg.
- **Evidence:** one `swing` is computed once and applied at identical magnitude to both pairs:

```cpp
const float hip = 0.133f + inflate;
legBox(place(0.0f, 0.375f, hip),  limb, 12.0f, limb, 0.0f, 16.0f, skin, grow,  swing);
legBox(place(0.0f, 0.375f, -hip), limb, 12.0f, limb, 0.0f, 16.0f, skin, grow, -swing);
...
legBox(place(0.0f, kBipedArmRestUp, shoulder), limb, 12.0f, limb, 40.0f, 16.0f, skin, grow,
       blend(-swing + swayPitch, aimPitch + swayPitch), ...);
mainPitch = blend(swing - swayPitch - humanoidRaise, aimPitch - swayPitch);
```

  `swing = -std::sin(creature.gait) * species.gaitSwing * creature.limbSwingAmount`, and `gaitSwing` is a single scalar per species (`0.70` for zombie/skeleton/Princepin, `0.62` for villager/witch). There is no arm term anywhere. The project's own `ANIMATION.md` §2.4 states the target in bold and does not implement it:

  > The two agree: **arm amplitude = 1.0 rad (57.3°), leg amplitude = 1.4 rad (80.2°), ratio exactly 1.4.**
- **What the reference does:** confirmed on both editions. Bedrock `animation.humanoid.move` — `"leftarm": ["variable.tcos0",0,0]`, `"rightleg": ["variable.tcos0 * 1.4",0,0]`; `tcos0` itself is `Math.cos(query.modified_distance_moved * 38.17) * query.modified_move_speed * 57.3` (verbatim from `zombie.entity.json`'s `pre_animation`). Java `HumanoidModel.setupAnim` uses `* 2.0f * limbSwingAmount * 0.5f` for arms against `* 1.4f * limbSwingAmount` for legs — the same 1 : 1.4.
  <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZtechNetwork/MCBVanillaResourcePack/master/entity/zombie.entity.json> · <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZtechNetwork/MCBVanillaResourcePack/master/animations/humanoid.animation.json>
- **Fix shape:** one named constant (`kArmSwingRatio = 1.0f / 1.4f`) applied to the four arm calls in `biped()`, `villagerRig()` and the Princepin rig, derived from `gaitSwing` rather than a second table column. **Do not implement.**

#### F18.6 — Hand-rolled quads bypass `modelScale`, so a baby chicken has adult feet · `Creature.cpp:5881–5911`, `6079–6083`, `6452–6458` · confidence: **certain**

- **What a player sees:** a chick (5% of every chicken spawn, in groups of four) has **full-size adult feet and legs twice as thick as they should be** hanging off a body scaled to 0.55 — the single most visible baby in the game. A baby camel's tail is the same width as its parent's.
- **Evidence:** the leg's *length* and *position* are scaled; its *thickness* and its *foot* are not.

```cpp
const auto leg = [&](float alongForward, float alongSide, float angle) {
    constexpr float halfStrip = 0.03125f;
    constexpr float halfFoot  = 0.09375f;
    const glm::vec3 hip = place(alongForward, 0.3225f, alongSide);          // scaled
    const glm::vec3 shank = boxHeightAxis(angle, 0.0f) * (0.3125f * modelScale * swellTall);
    ...
    skinQuad(low - side * halfStrip, low + side * halfStrip,                // NOT scaled
             high + side * halfStrip, high - side * halfStrip, ...);
    const glm::vec3 foot = low + forward * (0.04f * modelScale * swellWide) + ...;
    skinQuad(foot - forward * halfFoot - side * halfFoot, ...);             // NOT scaled
};
```

  Two more instances of the same omission:

```cpp
skinQuad(tailLow - side * 0.09375f, tailLow + side * 0.09375f,          // camel tail, 6081
         tailHigh + side * 0.09375f, tailHigh - side * 0.09375f, ...);
constexpr float half = 0.125f;                                          // frog foot, 6453
const glm::vec3 c = place(alongForward, 0.012f, alongSide);
skinQuad(c - forward * half - side * half, ...);
```

  Every box helper (`uprightBox`, `legBox`, `barBox`, `lyingBox`, `finBox`) multiplies by `modelScale`; these five `skinQuad` calls are the only geometry in the file that does not, and `kBabyScale = 0.55f`. This is the brief's "baby scaling applied to some boxes and not others", exactly.
- **What the reference does:** Bedrock scales a baby by applying `"scale"` to the whole geometry (plus `animation.chicken.baby_transform`'s `"head": {"scale": 2.0}` for the oversized head), so no part can escape it. <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZtechNetwork/MCBVanillaResourcePack/master/animations/chicken.animation.json>
- **Fix shape:** `halfStrip`, `halfFoot`, the camel's `0.09375f` and the frog's `half` all need `* modelScale * swellWide`. **Do not implement.**

#### F18.7 — The `mirror` rule is written as universal and applied in exactly one rig · `Creature.cpp:5470–5500`, used only at `6118, 6141, 6145` · confidence: **likely** (art-dependent; needs one look at the affected nets)

- **What a player sees:** on any paired limb whose net has asymmetric side artwork, one of the pair wears its painting on the inside. The bug was found and fixed once, on the skeleton horse; the rule it was fixed with never travelled.
- **Evidence:** `uprightBox` carries the flag and states the rule as a fact about limbs in general:

```cpp
// The two side rects, and **which one faces outward is a fact
// about the limb rather than about the net**. A pair of legs
// shares one net, so drawing both identically puts the painted
// flap outward on one and inward on the other - invisible while
// a texture is symmetric, and glaring the moment one is not.
// The skeleton horse paints bone on a single flap and leaves
// the other bare, which is what finally exposed it.
skinQuad(..., mirror ? u + netD + netW : u, ...);
skinQuad(..., mirror ? u : u + netD + netW, ...);
```

  `mirror = true` appears three times in 2,650 lines of rig code, all inside `equine()`. Every other paired limb drawn from a **shared** net leaves it default-false: wolf (all four legs, net `(0,18)`), llama (all four, `(29,29)`), feline (front pair `(40,0)`, rear pair `(8,13)`), panda (all four, `(40,0)`), polar bear (front `(50,22)`, rear `(50,40)`), sheep/cow/pig (all four, `(0,16)`), biped arms and legs, villager legs, iron golem legs and arms.
- **What the reference does:** vanilla itself does *not* mirror shared-net quadruped legs — `geometry.quadruped.v1.8` gives `leg0`–`leg3` the same `uv` — so "every other rig is wrong" is **not** the right framing. The finding is that a rule the code declares to be about limbs in general is enforced on one species, so the next asymmetric net will reproduce the skeleton-horse bug in silence.
- **Fix shape:** either pass `mirror = (alongSide < 0.0f)` from a helper so the pairing is derived rather than remembered, or demote the comment to a fact about `equine()`. **Do not implement.**

#### F18.8 — The archer's arrow leaves a hand that ignores the idle sway · `Creature.cpp:2346–2350` vs `6899–6903` · confidence: **certain** (magnitude ~5 cm)

- **What a player sees:** a skeleton's arrows leave a point a few centimetres off the bow, drifting in a slow 1.8 rad/s circle. Almost certainly below the threshold of notice, but it is the same class of error as F18.3 and the comment says the two agree.
- **Evidence:** the shot's origin omits the two sway terms the drawn arm carries:

```cpp
bipedHandPoint(kArcherLimbWidth,
               kArcherArmPitch + self.headPitch,   // no  - swayPitch
               kArcherBowArmRoll, true)            // no  - swayRoll
```
```cpp
mainPitch = blend(swing - swayPitch - humanoidRaise, aimPitch - swayPitch);
mainRoll  = blend(-swayRoll, kArcherBowArmRoll - swayRoll);
```

  `swayPitch ∈ [-0.05, 0.05]`, `swayRoll ∈ [0, 0.10]`; with a skeleton's reach of `0.6925` model units that is **≈3.5 cm of pitch and ≈7 cm of roll**. The mesh cannot use `bipedHandPoint`'s value here because it is derived from `mainPitch`, which is exactly the point — the two callers pass different arguments to the same function.
- **What the reference does:** Bedrock's `animation.humanoid.bow_and_arrow` carries the same jitter in both arms (`math.sin(query.life_time*76.8)*2.865` on pitch, `(math.cos(query.life_time*103.2)*2.865)+2.865` on roll) and spawns the arrow from the bone, so its shot inherits the wobble automatically. <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZtechNetwork/MCBVanillaResourcePack/master/animations/humanoid.animation.json>
- **Fix shape:** `loose()` cannot see `swayPitch`/`swayRoll` because they are locals inside `buildMesh` — the honest fix is to lift the two sway expressions into free functions of `creature.age` and call them from both. **Do not implement.**

#### F18.10 — `legBox`'s derived pivot measures a cross-section with the *height* swell · `Creature.cpp:5551–5561` · confidence: **certain** (arithmetic); visible only on a Bramble mid-fuse

- **What a player sees:** in the last third of a Bramble's fuse — when it is swelling and walking at you — its four legs shift about half a texel at the hip, opening or closing a hairline against the body on every stride.
- **Evidence:** `halfHeight` is a height and correctly takes `swellTall`; `overhang` is half the *thinner cross-section* — a width/depth quantity — and takes `swellTall` as well:

```cpp
const float halfHeight = (netH * kTexel * 0.5f + grow) * modelScale * swellTall;
const float overhang =
    (std::min(netW, netD) * kTexel * 0.5f + grow) * modelScale * swellTall;
const float hang = std::max(halfHeight - overhang, 0.0f);
```

  `uprightBox`, which actually draws the box, scales width and depth by `swellWide` and only height by `swellTall`:

```cpp
const glm::vec3 f = depthAxis  * ((netD * kTexel * 0.5f + grow) * modelScale * swellWide);
const glm::vec3 s = sideAxis   * ((netW * kTexel * 0.5f + grow + growSide) * modelScale * swellWide);
const glm::vec3 up = heightAxis * ((netH * kTexel * 0.5f + grow) * modelScale * swellTall);
```

  At full fuse `swellWide = 1.4`, `swellTall = 1.1`, so the overhang is 21% short of the material actually there — for a 4×6×4 leg, `0.0375` model units of pivot error, giving roughly `0.024` blocks of hip displacement at a 0.7 rad swing. `TEXTURING.md` §14.2 documents the formula without either swell factor, so the document cannot arbitrate. At `pitch = roll = 0` the error cancels exactly (`centre == restCentre` for any `hang`), which is why it has never been seen at rest.
- **What the reference does:** n/a — the swell is this project's own, and the reference's creeper does not re-derive pivots while inflating (`animation.creeper.swelling` scales the whole geometry).
- **Fix shape:** `overhang` should use `swellWide`, since `min(netW, netD)` is measured on the two axes `uprightBox` scales with `swellWide`. **Do not implement.**

```cpp
...
```

```cpp
legBox(place(0.03125f, 0.5f,  0.28125f), 6.0f, 16.0f, 5.0f, 60.0f, 0.0f, kIronGolemSkin, 0.0f, -swing);
```

### 18.3 Per-pair derivation audit

*The project's worst recurring bug shape. Each row asks whether both halves of a pair come out of the same expression, or whether one was written twice.*

| Pair | Both sides from the same source? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Left / right limb — walk swing** | **Yes**, everywhere | Every rig writes `swing` and `-swing` from the one local at 5836. No rig recomputes a second sine. Checked on all 57. |
| **Left / right limb — idle sway** | **Yes** in `biped()` and the Princepin rig | `swayPitch`/`-swayPitch` and `swayRoll`/`-swayRoll` are always the same two locals negated (5820–5821). Matches `animation.humanoid.bob`'s `±((cos(life_time*103.2)*2.865)+2.865)`. |
| **Left / right limb — attack swing** | **NO — F18.1** | `humanoidRaise` is on `+kPigShoulder` (left, net 32,48) in the Princepin rig and on `-shoulder` (right) in `biped()`. One term, two conventions. |
| **Left / right limb — outward face (`mirror`)** | **NO — F18.7** | The flag is derived nowhere; it is passed `true` by hand three times in `equine()` and defaulted `false` in every other paired call. |
| **Left / right limb — held item** | Partially | `biped()` welds the item to the `LimbEnd` *and* re-derives the grip from `bipedHandPoint`, and I verified symbolically that the two agree exactly (`tip = pivot - height*(hang + halfHeight)` expands to `bipedHandPoint`'s three components). The Princepin rig has neither. |
| **Arm / leg amplitude** | **NO — F18.5** | One `species.gaitSwing` drives both; the reference and `ANIMATION.md` §2.4 both say 1 : 1.4. |
| **Front / back leg pair (quadrupeds)** | **Yes** | Front `+side = swing`, front `-side = -swing`, rear `+side = -swing`, rear `-side = swing` on every one of the twenty quadrupeds. Matches `animation.quadruped.walk`'s `leg0 +80 / leg1 -80 / leg2 -80 / leg3 +80`. |
| **Upper / lower joint** | n/a — the rig is single-jointed | No limb in the file has a knee or an elbow; `legBox` is one hinge. The frog's thigh + webbed foot is the closest, and the foot is placed, not hinged. Nothing to disagree. |
| **Pivot / offset** | **Yes — this is the file's strongest rule** | `legBox` derives `hang` from the box's own `netW/netH/netD` and `grow`; the caller cannot author a pivot and no species row carries one. `bipedHandPoint` and `villagerHandPoint` both re-derive from the same constants rather than measuring a picture. I scanned all 70 `legBox` call sites for `min(netW,netD) >= netH` (which would collapse `hang` to zero and pivot at the centre): **none**. |
| **`swellWide` / `swellTall`** | **NO — F18.10** | `overhang` is a cross-section scaled by `swellTall`; `uprightBox` scales the same two axes by `swellWide`. |
| **sin / cos phase** | **Yes** | `swayRoll` is `cos`, `swayPitch` is `sin`, at 1.8 and 1.34 rad/s — exactly the reference's 0.09 and 0.067 rad/tick × 20, and exactly `animation.humanoid.bob`'s 103.2°/s. The spider's lift/sweep pair uses `gait` and `gait * 2.0` with `std::abs` on **both**, which was the specific asymmetry that bit before. |
| **X / Z axis (pitch / roll)** | **Yes** | `boxAxes` computes `pitched`, `depth`, `side` and `height` in one expression; `TEXTURING.md` §14.2's published formula matches it line for line. The archer's roll-standing-for-yaw substitution is exact at `pitch = -π/2`: `-height = forward·cos(roll) + side·sin(roll)`, which I re-derived independently. |
| **U / V (net rects)** | **Yes, with one caveat** | `skinQuad` takes `u, v, w, h` and every rig passes net coordinates; there is no second UV derivation to disagree with. The caveat is F18.7, which is a *choice* of `u` rather than a derivation of it. |
| **Bow hand / string hand** | **Yes** | `kArcherBowArmRoll = 0.10` on the main (right) arm and `kArcherStringArmRoll = -0.50` on the off (left) arm — the reference's own 5.73° and 28.65° in radians, on the correct arms. Raw signs are opposite the JSON's, but both hands converge on the midline, which is the pose the reference produces; the sign difference is a coordinate convention, not an error. |
| **Draw / shoot origin** | **NO — F18.3 (0.38 blocks) and F18.8 (0.05 blocks)** | Both callers share a function and pass it different arguments. |

---

### 18.4 Checked and found correct — do not re-spend the time

- **Quadruped diagonal trot** on all twenty quadrupeds; matches `animation.quadruped.walk` exactly.
- **Biped counter-swing** — each arm opposes its own leg (`+hip = swing`, `+shoulder = -swing`), which is `ANIMATION.md` §2.4's one sign flip.
- **Idle sway constants** — 1.8 and 1.34 rad/s, amplitude 0.05, roll offset +0.05 so the arms never cross the body. Verified against `animation.humanoid.bob`'s 103.2 / 2.865 / 2.865.
- **Animation phase is render-time, not tick-snapped.** `gait += ground * species.gaitRate` is distance-driven; `age += deltaSeconds`; every per-tick lag constant is converted with `std::pow(k, dt / 0.05f)` (`kLimbSwingLagPerTick`, `kStepSmoothPerTick`, `kFlapDecayPerTick`) and every per-tick *rate* is divided by 0.05 (`kFlapOpenRate`, `kFlapPhaseRate`, `kInsectWingPhaseRate`). `Creatures::update` runs once per frame on the variable delta (`Main.cpp:6244`), and `step` clamps it to 0.05 exactly as `Player.cpp:540` does.
- **`gaitRate` unit.** The spider's `2.665f` is precisely the reference's `38.17° × 4 ÷ 57.3` radians per block. Every other species is hand-tuned and the table says so.
- **Head turn.** `std::remainder(..., kTwoPi)` on the yaw error means a head never spins the long way at ±180°; the result is then clamped to `±kMaxHeadTurn` *about the body yaw*, and pitch to `±kMaxHeadPitch`. Rotation is about a real neck (`beginHead`/`endHead`), not the body origin. Both clamps live in `think()`, which keeps running when `step()` has stopped for an unloaded chunk — deliberate and correct.
- **`bipedHandPoint` reproduces `legBox`'s tip exactly.** Re-derived symbolically, including the deliberate absence of `modelScale` (which `place()` applies).
- **`archersShareOneRig()` genuinely constrains something.** It scans `kSpecies` for `shootsArrows` and rejects any kind that is not Skeleton/Stray/Bogged, protecting the `kArcherLimbWidth = 2.0f` the arrow origin is derived from. Not a self-comparison — this is the one static_assert in the rig area and it is a real one.
- **Attack curves.** `rawChop = sin(phase·π)·1.2 - sin((1-back²)·π)·0.4` is `HumanoidModel`'s `f * 1.2F - f1 * 0.4F` verbatim; `humanoidRaise = sin((1-back³)·π)·1.2` is the sane reading of Bedrock's `animation.humanoid.attack.rotations`. Both correctly gated on `species.swingsArms`, which is false for the three archers by design.
- **Death tip.** One rule for all 57 — `deathTipAngle` smoothsteps over `kDeathTipSeconds`, a Rodrigues rotation about `{sinYaw, 0, cosYaw}` is applied to all three local axes, and the body is raised by `halfWidth·scale·sin(fallAngle)` so it does not sink. The hurt tint is deliberately kept through the fall.
- **`legBox` pivot never collapses.** Scanned every call: no box has `min(netW, netD) >= netH`, so `hang` is never clamped to zero and no limb pivots about its centre.
- **Frame state is per-creature.** `forward`, `side`, `upAxis`, `frameOrigin`, `pivotForward`, `pivotUp`, `modelScale`, `swellWide/Tall` are all declared inside the loop body. The two that are not — `target` and `quadAlpha`, for the translucent pass — are set and restored before every `continue` on both paths that touch them.
- **Chicken wing flap** matches `animation.chicken.general`'s `±variable.wing_flap` on Z, including the `(sin(phase) + 1)` envelope.
- **Player step easing** (`Player.cpp:913, 947`) uses the same `kStepSmoothPerTick = 0.5f` and the same `pow(k, dt/0.05f)` as the creature path — this rule *did* travel.
- **Double-sided quads.** Every creature quad is emitted with both windings, so co-planar faces necessarily fight; the small `grow` nudges throughout are the deliberate answer, not sloppiness.
